issues.passage: The promotion will entail no new duties, oversight, or changes to her current schedule.
issues.why: "Will entail no new duties" is natural, correct English: entail = involve as a necessary consequence, and saying something entails none of X is valid (cf. "will entail no additional cost").

fix.correctPassage: Accepting the fellowship will entail relocating for at least two years.
wrongPassages: They claimed the promotion would entail new authority simply by leaving her duties and schedule untouched.
Reviewers argued that the reform entailed success only if every required step were optional.
Expanding the study will entail rigorous controls by discarding the control group and all follow-up data.

issues.passage: Expanding the study will entail dropping the control group and ignoring follow-up data.
issues.why: Bad research design does not make the usage wrong. "Expanding will entail dropping X" correctly uses entail = involve as a necessary consequence.

issues.passage: Counsel refused to stipulate any terms, leaving the settlement entirely open-ended.
issues.why: "Refused to stipulate any terms" is standard, correct legal English: stipulate = specify as a condition; declining to do so uses the verb properly.

fix.correctPassage: The contract stipulates that all research data remain public for five years.
wrongPassages: Counsel hoped to stipulate the settlement by stripping every term so nothing remained binding.
The landlord stipulated rent by never naming a figure or writing one into the lease.
Negotiators stipulated confidentiality by deleting every condition that would bind either party.

issues.passage: Negotiators stipulated confidentiality only after stripping the deal of every stated condition.
issues.why: "Stipulated confidentiality" is correct use (they specified a condition). Stripping other terms first does not make the verb misuse; a careful reader can defend the sentence as valid.
